subChunks.title: JDBC: Connecting & Querying

storyBeats.text: Eldrin opens a glowing portal to the Academy's great stone Archive — every wizard's record inscribed on tablets stretching to infinity.

storyBeats.speaker: Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: JDBC is the universal translation layer between Java and any relational database. Oracle, PostgreSQL, MySQL, H2 — the JDBC API is the same; only the driver and connection URL change. The four steps never vary: connect, prepare, execute, process.

storyBeats.label: JDBC in action

storyBeats.speaker: Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: Never build SQL strings with user input via concatenation. 'SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = \'' + userInput + '\'' — if userInput is ' OR '1'='1, you have just opened every record to the world. PreparedStatements seal that vulnerability.

guidedPractice.problemHtml: This exercise explains the JDBC pattern. Run the code to see the four-step summary printed.
guidedPractice.hint: The starter code demonstrates the JDBC pattern steps.

subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Describe the four steps of the JDBC pattern. Why must you always use PreparedStatement instead of Statement for user-supplied data?

questions.prompt: What is SQL injection and how does PreparedStatement prevent it?
options: User input is treated as data, not executable SQL — parameters are escaped automatically
SQL injection only affects INSERT statements
questions.answer: User input is treated as data, not executable SQL — parameters are escaped automatically
questions.explanation: PreparedStatement separates SQL structure from data. The ? placeholders are bound as values, never interpreted as SQL syntax — malicious input cannot alter the query structure.

subChunks.title: Transactions & Connection Pooling

storyBeats.text: The Academy treasurer transfers 100 gold from the scholarship fund to the apprentice fund — but the spell fails halfway. Without a transaction, the gold vanishes.

storyBeats.speaker: Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: A transaction is an all-or-nothing ward. Either every operation within it succeeds and commits, or an error triggers a rollback — every change undone, the data returned to its state before the transaction began. ACID: Atomic, Consistent, Isolated, Durable.

storyBeats.label: Transaction pattern

storyBeats.speaker: Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: HikariCP, the connection pool bundled with Spring Boot, is the fastest available. Without pooling, every request to your web application would spend 50ms just opening a database connection before doing any useful work. Pooling drops that to near-zero.

guidedPractice.problemHtml: Demonstrate the transaction pattern: simulate a successful transfer (two println operations then COMMITTED) and a failed transfer (ROLLED BACK with the failure message).
guidedPractice.hint: The starter code has transferDemo(false) for success and transferDemo(true) for simulated failure.

subChunks.feynmanPrompt: What are ACID properties of a database transaction? Why is connection pooling important for application performance?

options: Begins a manual transaction — changes are not committed until you call commit()
questions.answer: Begins a manual transaction — changes are not committed until you call commit()
questions.explanation: By default, each SQL statement auto-commits. Setting autoCommit(false) groups subsequent statements into a single transaction that you explicitly commit or rollback.

questions.prompt: A connection pool creates a new database connection for every request to improve reliability.
questions.explanation: A connection pool does the opposite — it maintains a set of pre-opened connections and reuses them. Creating new connections is expensive; pooling amortises that cost across many requests.
